catalogue.title: CS-101: Fundamentals of C
catalogue.summary: The language everything else was built on - compilation, memory, operators, branching and loops through to modular functions, with a real-life analogy, a video, and a scenario-based Compiler Quest for every one of 16 topics across 5 modules.

track.title: CS-101: Fundamentals of C
track.description: Absolute beginner to hardware-level understanding - the classic foundation language behind operating systems, databases, and almost every other language you will ever use. Five modules, sixteen topics, one real-life analogy and one scenario-based Compiler Quest each - from how a compiler turns source into machine code, through memory, operators and branching, to loops and modular functions - certificate at the end.
track.outcome: Understand the compilation lifecycle, program structure, memory-typed variables and formatted input/output; use relational/logical operators and branching to make decisions; use for/while loops and loop controls to repeat and manage work; write function prototypes, understand pass-by-value, and use return types (including void) to build modular programs.

levels.title: The C Compilation Lifecycle
levels.topic:
Real-life analogy: Think of an architect drawing a blueprint in English. A construction robot that only responds to raw electrical pulses cannot read English words - a precision translator (the Compiler) validates the blueprint syntax and translates every single instruction into binary machine code before construction starts.

Computers execute instructions in machine language (binary 0s and 1s). The C compiler translates human-readable source code (.c) through 4 stages: Preprocessing (expanding headers like #include <stdio.h>), Compilation (translating C to assembly), Assembly (converting assembly to machine object code), and Linking (combining object code with system libraries into a runnable executable).

problems.title: Airport Gate Terminal Initialization
problems.description:
Write a minimal C program that compiles cleanly and outputs the gate initialization confirmation message to the standard console, exactly like an airport terminal boots up and confirms it's online before passengers arrive.

Input: None
Expected Output:
Gate 14B: System Online
criteria: The program compiles through all 4 stages without error (correct #include, main(), and syntax)
The exact line "Gate 14B: System Online" is printed, nothing more, nothing less
problems.hint: A single printf("Gate 14B: System Online\n"); inside main() is all this needs.

levels.title: Anatomy of main() and Program Entry
levels.topic:
Real-life analogy: Think of entering an automated factory. No matter how large the facility is, operations always initiate through a single designated master control switch labeled "Gate 1: Entry Point" - the main() function is that universal entry point.

Every C program must have exactly one int main() function. The int keyword indicates that the program reports an exit status integer back to the Operating System. The code block boundaries are defined by curly braces { }, each statement must terminate with a semicolon ;, and return 0; indicates standard error-free termination.

problems.title: Server Handshake Status
problems.description:
Create a structured C source file containing the standard main() block and return code that outputs a server handshake status, the way a server confirms a clean connection before any data flows.

Input: None
Expected Output:
Server Handshake: 200 OK
criteria: Exactly one int main() function exists, with curly-brace boundaries and every statement ending in a semicolon
The function ends with return 0; after printing the exact handshake line
problems.hint: printf("Server Handshake: 200 OK\n"); then return 0; inside int main() { ... }.

levels.title: Standard Output & Escape Sequences
levels.topic:
Real-life analogy: Think of an office typewriter with carriage-return and tab levers. Typing without the levers puts all text on a single messy line - hitting the return lever moves down to a fresh line, while hitting the tab key aligns items into neat columns.

The printf() function prints text to standard console output. Escape sequences prefixed by a backslash allow layout formatting: \n inserts a newline character, \t creates a tab-stop gap, and \" prints a literal double quote.

problems.title: Cafe POS Itemized Receipt
problems.description:
Use a single printf() statement with escape sequences (\n and \t) to print a multi-line, tab-aligned receipt header and line items, the way a cafe's point-of-sale printer lines up an itemized bill.

Input: None
Expected Output:
ITEM\tQTY\tCOST
Espresso\t2\t$6.00
Muffin\t1\t$3.50
criteria: Every line break comes from \n and every column gap from \t inside ONE printf() call, not multiple calls or literal spaces
The three output lines and their tab-separated columns match exactly, in order
problems.hint:
One printf("ITEM	QTY	COST
Espresso	2	$6.00
Muffin	1	$3.50
"); does the whole receipt.

levels.title: Primitive Data Types & Memory Footprint
levels.topic:
Real-life analogy: Think of specialized kitchen containers - a small spice jar for salt (1 byte for a char), a mid-sized jug for milk (4 bytes for an integer), and a large tank for water reserves (8 bytes for a high-precision double).

C requires explicit data type declarations to allocate memory in RAM: int allocates 4 bytes for whole numbers (-2 billion to +2 billion), float allocates 4 bytes for 6-decimal-place numbers, double allocates 8 bytes for 15-decimal-place precision, and char allocates 1 byte for an ASCII character.

problems.title: Patient Intake Triage Card
problems.description:
Declare an integer for age (28), a double for body temperature (98.6), and a char for blood group ('O'). Print each on a new line, the way a hospital triage card records a patient's vitals in the right-sized container for each value.

Input: None (Hardcoded)
Expected Output:
Age: 28
Temp: 98.600000
Blood Group: O
criteria: age is declared int, temperature double, and blood group char - never the wrong container for the value
Each is printed with the matching format specifier (%d, %f, %c) producing exactly the 3 lines shown
problems.hint: double defaults to 6 decimal places with %f, so 98.6 prints as 98.600000 - that is expected, not a bug.

levels.title: Variable Declaration, Initialization & Constants
levels.topic:
Real-life analogy: Renting a gym locker is declaration - the locker is reserved in your name, but dirty clothes from the last user might be inside (garbage value). Putting your clean gear inside is initialization. Adding a permanent master padlock is declaring it const.

Declaring a variable allocates RAM but leaves whatever random leftover bits were previously stored at that address. Initializing (int count = 0;) ensures predictable behavior. The const keyword marks a variable as read-only; any subsequent reassignment causes a compiler error.

problems.title: Fixed Toll Plaza Billing
problems.description:
Declare a const int toll rate of 50. Declare an integer vehicles initialized to 4. Compute total revenue and print formatted results, the way a toll plaza's rate never changes mid-shift but the vehicle count does.

Input: None
Expected Output:
Toll Rate: 50
Vehicles: 4
Total Revenue: 200
criteria: tollRate is declared const int and vehicles is a plain, initialized int (never left uninitialized)
Total Revenue is computed as tollRate * vehicles and prints as exactly 200
problems.hint: const int tollRate = 50; int vehicles = 4; then print tollRate * vehicles for the total.

levels.title: Format Specifiers
levels.topic:
Real-life analogy: Think of 3D optical filter glasses - the raw screen emits mixed light, but wearing red/cyan lenses lets your eyes decode the exact intended 3D visual. Format specifiers are the decoding lenses that tell printf how to interpret binary data.

Binary data in memory needs interpretation rules: %d formats integers, %f formats floats, %.2f rounds and formats floating-point values to 2 decimal places, and %c displays single character symbols.

problems.title: Precision Currency Formatter
problems.description:
Take a raw unrounded float value 129.8765 and print it formatted to 2 decimal places preceded by a dollar sign, the way a checkout receipt always shows exactly two decimal places for money, never four.

Input: None
Expected Output:
Final Charge: $129.88
criteria: The format specifier is %.2f, not the default %f (which would print 6 decimals)
129.8765 rounds correctly to 129.88 (not truncated to 129.87), with the dollar sign printed literally
problems.hint: printf("Final Charge: $%.2f\n", 129.8765); - %.2f both rounds and limits to 2 decimals.

levels.title: Interactive Input with scanf()
levels.topic:
Real-life analogy: When a courier delivers a parcel, you don't just describe the package - you must provide your exact physical street address so the parcel is dropped directly at your doorstep. The & symbol gives scanf() your variable's memory address.

The scanf() function reads characters from the Standard Input (stdin) stream. Because scanf() must write incoming data directly into your variable's memory cell in RAM, it requires the memory address obtained using the address-of operator &.

problems.title: ATM Cash Withdrawal Prompt
problems.description:
Read an integer withdrawal amount from input using scanf() and print an execution confirmation message, exactly like an ATM confirms the amount before dispensing cash.

Sample Input: 500
Expected Output:
Processing withdrawal for $500. Dispensing cash...
criteria: scanf("%d", &amount); includes the & before the variable name, or it would write to a random memory spot
The confirmation line embeds the exact scanned value, matching the sample output for input 500
problems.hint: scanf("%d", &amount); then printf("Processing withdrawal for $%d. Dispensing cash...\n", amount);

levels.title: Arithmetic & Modulo Operations
levels.topic:
Real-life analogy: If you divide 11 apples among 2 people, each person gets 5 whole apples (integer division 11 / 2 = 5), and 1 single apple remains in the basket (modulo remainder 11 % 2 = 1).

Arithmetic in C follows standard math rules, but integer division truncates decimal fractions completely without rounding. The modulo operator % yields the integer remainder after division, making it essential for cyclic events, parity tests, and time calculations.

problems.title: Warehouse Cargo Box Packer
problems.description:
A shipping crate holds 6 items. Read an integer total of items from input, compute packed crates and leftover loose items - the same way a warehouse worker fills full crates first and sets the remainder aside.

Sample Input: 29
Expected Output:
Full Crates: 4
Remaining Items: 5
criteria: Full crates use integer division (total / 6) and remaining items use modulo (total % 6), not the other way round
For input 29, the program prints exactly "Full Crates: 4" and "Remaining Items: 5"
problems.hint: crates = total / 6; leftover = total % 6;

levels.title: Relational & Logical Decisions
levels.topic:
Real-life analogy: An airport security check requires: "Do you have a passport (Condition 1) AND a boarding pass (Condition 2)?" If both are verified true, you pass through the gate - if either is missing, access is denied.

C treats 0 as False and any non-zero integer as True. Relational operators (<, >, ==, !=) yield 1 or 0. Logical AND (&&) requires all conditions to be true, Logical OR (||) requires at least one to be true, and Logical NOT (!) inverts truth values.

problems.title: Theme Park Ride Safety Gate
problems.description:
Read height (cm) and age as two space-separated integers. Print Eligibility: 1 if height is at least 120 AND age is at least 10, otherwise print Eligibility: 0 - exactly like a ride's safety gate checks both conditions together before letting anyone through.

Sample Input: 135 12
Expected Output:
Eligibility: 1
criteria: Both conditions are combined with && (logical AND), not evaluated or printed separately
For input "135 12" the program prints exactly "Eligibility: 1"
problems.hint: if (height >= 120 && age >= 10) printf("Eligibility: 1\n"); else printf("Eligibility: 0\n");

levels.title: Branching with if, else if, and else
levels.topic:
Real-life analogy: Think of a train reaching an automated track switch. If the signal is green, the switch steers onto Track 1. If yellow, it steers onto Track 2. In any other condition, it diverts to the safety siding.

The if statement checks a condition. If true, its block executes and all alternate branches are bypassed. If false, control passes sequentially through each else if block. If all tests fail, the default else fallback block executes.

problems.title: Smart Thermostat Temperature Alert
problems.description:
Read an integer Celsius temperature. Print ALERT: HIGH if it is above 35, ALERT: LOW if it is below 15, and STATUS: NORMAL otherwise - the same three-way branch a smart thermostat runs on every reading.

Sample Input: 38
Expected Output:
ALERT: HIGH
criteria: The three outcomes are chained as if / else if / else, not three separate independent if statements
For input 38 the program prints exactly "ALERT: HIGH", and only one branch ever runs per input
problems.hint: if (temp > 35) ... else if (temp < 15) ... else printf("STATUS: NORMAL\n");

levels.title: Counter-Controlled for Loops
levels.topic:
Real-life analogy: A running coach instructs an athlete: "Run 5 laps around the track. Start at lap 1, add 1 lap every time you cross the line, and stop after lap 5." The start, step, and stop counts are all defined upfront.

When the total number of iterations is known before loop entry, a for loop consolidates loop setup: for (initialization; condition; update). The initialization runs once, the condition is evaluated before each iteration, and the update statement executes after each loop body run.

problems.title: Rocket Launch Countdown
problems.description:
Read an integer start value from input and count down to 1 using a for loop, followed by LIFTOFF! - the same fixed, known-in-advance countdown every rocket launch runs.

Sample Input: 5
Expected Output:
5 4 3 2 1 LIFTOFF!
criteria: A for loop counts down from the input value to 1 (the iteration count is known upfront, matching a for loop, not a while loop)
The numbers print space-separated on one line, followed immediately by "LIFTOFF!"
problems.hint: for (int i = start; i >= 1; i--) printf("%d ", i); then printf("LIFTOFF!\n");

levels.title: Condition-Driven while Loops
levels.topic:
Real-life analogy: You don't decide in advance to hold an umbrella for exactly 350 steps - you check the sky and keep holding it while rain continues to fall. When the rain stops, you close the umbrella.

A while loop is used when the number of cycles is indeterminate and driven by runtime events or changing data values. It tests the condition before executing the body - if the condition is false initially, the loop never runs.

problems.title: EV Fast-Charging Battery Monitor
problems.description:
Read an integer starting battery level. Increment it by 10% in a while loop until the level reaches or exceeds 100%, then print the final percentage - the same open-ended charge cycle an EV's battery monitor runs, whose length depends entirely on the starting level.

Sample Input: 75
Expected Output:
Charging complete: 105%
criteria: A while loop repeats the +10% step only while level < 100, since the number of cycles is not known in advance
For a starting level of 75, the loop runs until it lands on exactly 105% (75 -> 85 -> 95 is still under 100, so a third +10 step is required) and prints "Charging complete: 105%"
problems.hint: while (level < 100) { level += level * 0.10; } then print the final level - it will overshoot past 100, which is expected.

levels.title: Loop Controls (break & continue)
levels.topic:
Real-life analogy: On a bottling line, if an empty bottle passes by, the labeler skips it and moves to the next bottle (continue). But if a glass bottle shatters on the conveyor, the operator hits the emergency stop button immediately (break).

The break statement causes immediate termination of the innermost loop, transferring control to the next statement outside the loop. The continue statement skips all remaining lines in the current iteration and jumps directly to the next loop evaluation.

problems.title: Inventory Defect Scanner
problems.description:
Read count N, then N item codes. Print valid positive codes. Skip code 0 using continue. Halt immediately on a negative code with break and print HALTED - exactly like a scanner skips an empty slot but emergency-stops on a damaged item.

Sample Input:
5
101 0 102 -1 103
Expected Output:
101 102 HALTED
criteria: Code 0 is skipped with continue (never printed), while a negative code triggers break immediately, stopping before any later codes are read
For the sample input the program prints exactly "101 102 HALTED", never reaching 103
problems.hint: if (code == 0) continue; if (code < 0) { printf("HALTED\n"); break; } else printf("%d ", code);

levels.title: Function Declarations & Prototypes
levels.topic:
Real-life analogy: Think of a restaurant menu summary. Before the kitchen prepares dishes described further down in the detailed kitchen binder, the customer reads the menu title and ingredients at the front - the prototype announces what exists before use.

C compilers scan files sequentially from top to bottom. If a function is called before its full definition is reached, the compiler raises an undeclared error. A function prototype placed at the top declares the function's name, return type, and parameter list in advance.

problems.title: Temperature Unit Converter Module
problems.description:
Declare the prototype float toFahrenheit(float c); at the top of the file. Define the actual function below main(). Read a float Celsius value and print it converted to Fahrenheit, formatted to 1 decimal place - just like the menu announces the dish before the kitchen binder defines how to make it.

Sample Input: 25.0
Expected Output:
77.0 F
criteria: A prototype float toFahrenheit(float c); appears above main(), with the full definition placed below main()
The formula (c * 9/5) + 32 is used, and the result prints with exactly 1 decimal place followed by " F" (77.0 F for input 25.0)
problems.hint: float toFahrenheit(float c) { return (c * 9.0/5.0) + 32; } - print with %.1f.

levels.title: Pass-by-Value & Parameter Passing
levels.topic:
Real-life analogy: If you give a classmate a photocopy of your notes and they scribble calculations on it, the original master copy safely in your backpack remains completely clean and unchanged.

C uses Pass-by-Value by default. When passing variables to functions, a separate temporary copy is created in that function's stack frame. Modifying the parameter inside the function alters only the local copy, leaving the original variable in main() intact.

problems.title: Coupon Discount Scope Verification
problems.description:
Write a function void applyPromo(int val) that subtracts 20 from val. In main(), initialize price = 100, call applyPromo(price), and print price in main() afterward - proving the photocopy (the parameter) was scribbled on, not the original.

Input: None
Expected Output:
Original Price in main: 100
criteria: applyPromo(int val) modifies only its local parameter val, never anything declared in main()
After calling applyPromo(price), main()'s price is printed and is still exactly 100 - proving pass-by-value
problems.hint: void applyPromo(int val) { val -= 20; } - calling it can never change price back in main().

levels.title: Return Types & Void Functions
levels.topic:
Real-life analogy: Asking an accountant to compute net profit yields a specific financial figure back (return value). Asking an office assistant to ring the fire alarm executes an emergency routine without handing you a calculation (void function).

A function's return type dictates the type of data sent back to the caller via the return statement. When a function executes actions (such as logging warnings, playing tones, or formatting screens) without computing a return value, its return type is declared as void.

problems.title: Emergency Siren Dispatcher
problems.description:
Write a function void triggerAlert(int code) that prints a formatted emergency dispatch notice. Read an integer code and call the function - the capstone finale, combining everything from functions to formatted output into one dispatch routine, exactly like an office assistant rings the alarm without returning any figure back.

Sample Input: 404
Expected Output:
*** EMERGENCY ALERT: CODE 404 ACTIVE ***
criteria: triggerAlert is declared void (it performs an action and returns nothing) and is called with the scanned code
For input 404 the exact line "*** EMERGENCY ALERT: CODE 404 ACTIVE ***" is printed, with the code value correctly embedded
problems.hint: void triggerAlert(int code) { printf("*** EMERGENCY ALERT: CODE %d ACTIVE ***\n", code); }

catalogue.title: CS-102: Fundamentals of C++ (with OOP)
catalogue.summary: Streams and iostream, modern types (auto/const), std::string and std::vector, references and overloading, through to encapsulated classes with constructors, destructors and validated getters/setters.

track.title: CS-102: Fundamentals of C++ (with Object-Oriented Programming)
track.description: Modern C++ from streams to objects - stronger type safety, namespaces, references, the STL, and encapsulated classes with constructors and destructors. Four modules, twelve topics, one real-life analogy, one video and one scenario-based Compiler Quest each - certificate at the end.
track.outcome: Use iostream, namespaces and type-safe std::cin/std::cout streams; work with modern types (auto, const), std::string and std::vector; write range-based for loops, use references for direct in-place mutation, and overload functions by signature; design encapsulated classes with private state, public methods, constructors, destructors and validated getters/setters.

levels.title: C++ Compilation & iostream
levels.topic:
Real-life analogy: Think of upgrading an old mechanical typewriter to an automated publishing console. Instead of manually feeding characters, you connect an organized communication tube (iostream) that handles bidirectional text pipelines smoothly.

C++ builds on C with stronger type safety, namespaces, and object abstractions. The preprocessor header #include <iostream> provides access to the standard input/output stream objects. Code is compiled by modern C++ compilers (like g++ or clang++) into high-performance native executables.

problems.title: System Terminal Initializer
problems.description:
Write a clean C++ program that initializes the standard stream and prints a system boot confirmation - the mechanical typewriter finally connected to its automated publishing console.

Input: None
Expected Output:
C++ Engine: Core Initialized
criteria: #include <iostream> is present and the program compiles as valid C++ (an int main() with return 0;)
The exact line "C++ Engine: Core Initialized" is printed, nothing more, nothing less
problems.hint: #include <iostream>\nint main() { std::cout << "C++ Engine: Core Initialized" << std::endl; return 0; }

levels.title: Namespaces & std::cout
levels.topic:
Real-life analogy: In a school with two students named "Alex," calling "Alex" creates confusion. Adding their family surname - "Smith::Alex" or "Miller::Alex" - identifies the exact person. A namespace prevents name collisions across large software libraries.

C++ organizes standard library symbols inside the std namespace. We access output streams using the scope resolution operator as std::cout with the stream insertion operator <<. The stream manipulator std::endl inserts a newline and immediately flushes the terminal output buffer.

problems.title: Scoped Banner Generator
problems.description:
Use std::cout and std::endl to output a 2-line scoped status report without using using namespace std; globally - properly scoping every call like addressing students by their full "Surname::Name".

Input: None
Expected Output:
Namespace: STD Verified
Status: 200 Ready
criteria: Every std library call is fully scoped as std::cout / std::endl - using namespace std; does not appear anywhere in the file
The program prints exactly the two lines "Namespace: STD Verified" and "Status: 200 Ready", in that order
problems.hint: std::cout << "Namespace: STD Verified" << std::endl; std::cout << "Status: 200 Ready" << std::endl;

levels.title: std::cin Stream Input
levels.topic:
Real-life analogy: Think of a mail conveyor belt pointing straight into your sorting bin. The stream extraction operator >> points toward the variable, seamlessly directing whatever comes off the conveyor directly into that storage slot without needing memory addresses.

Unlike C's scanf which requires memory format specifiers (%d) and ampersands (&), C++ uses type-safe stream extraction with std::cin >> var. The compiler automatically determines variable types at compile-time and extracts tokens separated by whitespace.

problems.title: User Verification Scanner
problems.description:
Read an integer user ID and a double account balance using std::cin. Print them formatted using std::cout - the conveyor belt directing each token straight into its matching storage slot, no format specifiers or ampersands needed.

Sample Input: 108 2450.75
Expected Output:
User: 108 | Balance: $2450.75
criteria: Both values are read with std::cin >> (never scanf or a C-style format specifier), directly into a typed int and a typed double
For input "108 2450.75" the program prints exactly "User: 108 | Balance: $2450.75"
problems.hint: std::cin >> userId >> balance; then std::cout << "User: " << userId << " | Balance: $" << balance << std::endl;

levels.title: Types, auto & const
levels.topic:
Real-life analogy: A smart digital scale automatically knows whether it is measuring grams or kilograms based on what you drop onto the sensor plate. The auto keyword lets the compiler deduce the exact type automatically from its initial assignment value.

C++ includes standard primitives (int, double, char, bool with literal true/false). Modern C++ introduces auto for automatic type deduction at compile-time. Constants declared with const or constexpr enforce compile-time immutability and optimize runtime memory layout.

problems.title: Auto-Deduction Tax Calculator
problems.description:
Declare a const double TAX_RATE = 0.08. Read an integer price, compute the total using an auto total variable, and print the calculated cost - the compiler weighing the value on the sensor plate and deducing its type automatically.

Sample Input: 100
Expected Output:
Total with Tax: 108
criteria: TAX_RATE is declared const double (never reassigned), and total is declared with auto rather than an explicit type
For input 100 the program prints exactly "Total with Tax: 108"
problems.hint: const double TAX_RATE = 0.08; auto total = price + (price * TAX_RATE);

levels.title: std::string & Operations
levels.topic:
Real-life analogy: A traditional C-string is like individual wooden alphabet blocks glued to a fixed 10-slot plank (it can easily overflow). A std::string is like magnetic alphabet letters on an infinitely expandable strip that grows or shrinks automatically.

The std::string class provides dynamic, memory-managed string handling. It supports intuitive concatenation with the + operator, size querying via .length(), and robust line extraction with std::getline(std::cin, str) to read entire sentences with spaces.

problems.title: Full Name Badge Concatenator
problems.description:
Read two strings (first name and last name), concatenate them with a space using +, and print the full name with its total character count - two magnetic-letter strips joined onto one infinitely expandable badge.

Sample Input: Ada Lovelace
Expected Output:
Badge: Ada Lovelace (Length: 12)
criteria: The two names are joined with the + operator into one std::string (not printed as two separate std::cout calls with a literal space between)
The length shown is the concatenated string's own .length(), and for input "Ada Lovelace" the program prints exactly "Badge: Ada Lovelace (Length: 12)"
problems.hint: std::string full = first + " " + last; then use full.length() for the count.

levels.title: std::vector Dynamic Arrays
levels.topic:
Real-life analogy: Think of an accordion filing folder. When you add a new document, the folder stretches open another pocket automatically. You never need to declare a fixed size in advance.

The std::vector<T> is a sequential, contiguous dynamic container from the Standard Template Library (STL). Elements are appended dynamically at the end in O(1) amortized time using .push_back(), indexed safely using .at() or [], and queried with .size().

problems.title: Real-Time Score Tracker
problems.description:
Read count N, then N integers into a std::vector<int> using push_back. Print the vector size and the last element using .back() - the accordion folder stretching open one new pocket per score, with no fixed size declared in advance.

Sample Input:
3
45 88 92
Expected Output:
Entries: 3 | Latest: 92
criteria: Every value is added with .push_back() into a std::vector<int> - no fixed-size C-style array is declared
The output uses .size() and .back() directly (not a manually-tracked counter or arr[N-1]), printing exactly "Entries: 3 | Latest: 92" for the sample input
problems.hint: scores.push_back(n); ... std::cout << "Entries: " << scores.size() << " | Latest: " << scores.back();

levels.title: Range-based for Loops
levels.topic:
Real-life analogy: Think of a conveyor belt at airport baggage claim. Instead of counting "Bag 0, Bag 1, Bag 2," you simply stand in place and say "For every bag that rolls past me on this belt, inspect it."

Modern C++ (C++11 and beyond) introduces range-based for loops: for (const auto& item : container). This eliminates manual indexing, off-by-one errors, and boundary checks by iterating directly over every element in an array, string, or vector cleanly.

problems.title: Range Loop Sequence Summer
problems.description:
Read 4 integers into a vector, calculate their sum using a range-based for (auto num : vec) loop, and print the total - standing at the baggage belt and inspecting every bag that rolls past, with no manual index counting.

Sample Input: 10 20 30 40
Expected Output:
Sequence Sum: 100
criteria: The sum is accumulated using a range-based for (auto num : vec) loop - no index variable (i, vec[i]) appears in the summation
For input "10 20 30 40" the program prints exactly "Sequence Sum: 100"
problems.hint: int sum = 0; for (auto num : vec) sum += num;

levels.title: C++ References (&ref)
levels.topic:
Real-life analogy: Think of a nickname. "Robert" and "Bob" are two different names referring to the exact same human being. Giving Robert a glass of water is identical to giving Bob a glass of water.

A reference (int& ref = x;) creates an alias for an existing variable. Unlike raw pointers, references cannot be NULL, cannot be uninitialized, and cannot be reseated to point to another object. They provide direct memory access with clean syntax without dereferencing syntax (*).

problems.title: In-Place Reference Doubler
problems.description:
Implement void doubleValue(int& num) using reference semantics. Read an integer, pass it by reference to double it, and print the original variable in main() - Robert and Bob really are the same person, so doubling Bob's water doubles Robert's too.

Sample Input: 24
Expected Output:
Doubled Value: 48
criteria: doubleValue(int& num) takes its parameter by reference (&), and modifies num directly inside the function - no return value is used to pass the doubled result back
After calling doubleValue(x), main()'s own x prints as exactly "Doubled Value: 48" for input 24, proving the reference reached the original variable
problems.hint: void doubleValue(int& num) { num *= 2; } - called simply as doubleValue(x);, no & needed at the call site.

levels.title: Function Overloading
levels.topic:
Real-life analogy: Think of the word "Charge." If you are at an electronics store, "charge" means plug in a battery. If you are at a checkout counter, "charge" means debit an invoice. The context and parameters dictate the exact action.

In C++, multiple functions can share the exact same name as long as their parameter lists differ in type or count. The compiler performs overload resolution at compile-time by inspecting argument signatures, eliminating ugly C-style workarounds like printInt(), printFloat().

problems.title: Overloaded Area Calculator
problems.description:
Write two overloaded functions: int area(int side) for a square, and int area(int length, int width) for a rectangle. Compute and print both results based on input - the same word "area" meaning something different depending on how many arguments hand it.

Sample Input: 5 4 6
Expected Output:
Square: 25 | Rectangle: 24
criteria: Both functions share the exact name area, distinguished only by their parameter count (int area(int side) vs int area(int length, int width))
For input "5 4 6" the program prints exactly "Square: 25 | Rectangle: 24" (side=5 -> 25, length=4 width=6 -> 24)
problems.hint: int area(int side) { return side*side; } int area(int length, int width) { return length*width; }

levels.title: Classes, Objects & Access
levels.topic:
Real-life analogy: Think of an ATM machine. The money vault inside is private (customers cannot open it directly). The keypad and cash slot are public (authorized interfaces that safely interact with the internal cash).

A class is a blueprint that combines state (member variables) and behavior (member methods). Encapsulation is enforced using access specifiers: private members are hidden from external access, while public members expose the safe interaction interface.

problems.title: Encapsulated Bank Account
problems.description:
Create a BankAccount class with private double balance and public methods deposit(double amt) and getBalance(). Process a deposit and print the updated balance - the vault stays private, only the keypad-and-slot interface is exposed.

Sample Input: 150.50
Expected Output:
Account Balance: $150.50
criteria: balance is declared under private: and can only be read/changed through the public deposit() and getBalance() methods - no direct outside access to balance
For input 150.50 the program prints exactly "Account Balance: $150.50" after calling deposit()
problems.hint: class BankAccount { private: double balance = 0; public: void deposit(double amt) { balance += amt; } double getBalance() { return balance; } };

levels.title: Constructors & Destructors
levels.topic:
Real-life analogy: Buying a new smartphone automatically runs its initial setup wizard (a Constructor). When the phone is recycled years later, its internal storage is factory wiped clean (a Destructor).

A Constructor has the same name as the class and runs automatically when an object is instantiated to initialize member variables. A Destructor (prefixed with ~) runs automatically when the object goes out of scope to release resources (the RAII pattern).

problems.title: Device Lifecycle Logger
problems.description:
Write a Device class whose constructor prints "Device [NAME] Online" and destructor prints "Device [NAME] Offline" when exiting scope - the setup wizard running automatically at creation, and the factory wipe running automatically at the end.

Sample Input: RouterX
Expected Output:
Device RouterX Online
Device RouterX Offline
criteria: The Online line is printed from inside the constructor and the Offline line from inside the destructor (~Device()) - neither is printed manually from main()
For input "RouterX" the two lines print automatically in that exact order as the object is created and then goes out of scope
problems.hint: Device(std::string n) : name(n) { std::cout << "Device " << name << " Online" << std::endl; } ~Device() { std::cout << "Device " << name << " Offline" << std::endl; }

levels.title: Getters, Setters & 'this'
levels.topic:
Real-life analogy: A car's speedometer dial gives you a view of current speed (a Getter), while the gas pedal adjusts speed within safe engine limits (a Setter). The car's internal engine computer knows it is regulating this specific vehicle.

Getters and Setters provide controlled access to private members, enforcing validation rules before updating state. The hidden this pointer points to the current calling object instance, allowing explicit disambiguation between member variables and constructor parameters.

problems.title: Validated Speed Governor
problems.description:
Create a Car class with a private speed. A setter setSpeed(int speed) caps speed at 120 if the input exceeds 120. Read a speed integer and print the validated speed via a getter - the gas pedal that refuses to push the engine computer past its safe limit. The capstone finale, combining encapsulation, validation and the this pointer into one governor.

Sample Input: 145
Expected Output:
Governed Speed: 120 km/h
criteria: setSpeed(int speed) validates and caps the value at 120 BEFORE storing it in the private member (using this->speed = ... to disambiguate from the parameter), never storing the raw uncapped input
For input 145 the getter reports exactly "Governed Speed: 120 km/h", proving the cap was enforced
problems.hint: void setSpeed(int speed) { this->speed = (speed > 120) ? 120 : speed; }

catalogue.title: CS-104: Fundamentals of Python
catalogue.summary: The bytecode interpreter and dynamic typing through strings, control flow and core data structures to functions, classes and safe file I/O, with a real-life analogy, a video, and a scenario-based Compiler Quest for every one of 15 topics across 5 modules.

track.title: CS-104: Fundamentals of Python
track.description: Absolute beginner to working Python - the highest-demand first language, from the bytecode interpreter and dynamic typing through strings, control flow and core data structures to functions, classes and safe file I/O. Five modules, fifteen topics, one real-life analogy, one video and one scenario-based Compiler Quest each, every quest with an exact Sample Input and Expected Output - certificate at the end.
track.outcome: Use the Python interpreter and print() formatting, dynamic variables and input() casting to drive an interactive program; slice strings and build f-strings, and branch and loop over data with if/elif/else and for/while; model data with lists, comprehensions, tuples, sets and dictionaries; write functions with default and variable arguments and lambdas; design classes with __init__, inheritance and method overriding, and read and write files safely with with and try/except.

levels.title: Python Interpreter & print()
levels.topic:
Real-life analogy: Think of a live simultaneous translator reading a speech line-by-line, speaking each sentence as it arrives - never waiting for the whole book to be printed and bound first.

Python runs on a bytecode interpreter that executes your source one statement at a time, so there is no separate compile-and-link step to wait through. The print() function sends formatted text to standard output; its sep parameter sets what goes between multiple arguments (a space by default) and its end parameter sets what finishes the line (a newline by default).

problems.title: System Diagnostic Banner
problems.description:
Print a startup message, then on the next line print the three diagnostic tags CPU, MEM and DISK joined by a dash using print()'s sep parameter - the way a machine prints a boot banner and self-check before it comes online.

Input: None
Expected Output:
Booting Python Engine
CPU-MEM-DISK
criteria: The three tags are joined with print("CPU", "MEM", "DISK", sep="-"), not a hand-typed "CPU-MEM-DISK" string or + concatenation
The output is exactly two lines: "Booting Python Engine" then "CPU-MEM-DISK", nothing more
problems.hint: print("Booting Python Engine") then print("CPU", "MEM", "DISK", sep="-").

levels.title: Dynamic Variables & Types
levels.topic:
Real-life analogy: Think of a universal storage bin. You peel off the old label sticker and put on a new one whenever you want - today it holds shoes, tomorrow books, the day after coins - the bin never cares what type of thing goes in.

Python variables are names that refer to objects on the heap, and the same name can be rebound to a value of a different type at any time - you never declare a type. The core primitives are int (whole numbers), float (decimals) and bool (True / False), and type(x) reports which one an object is.

problems.title: Inventory Price Multiplier
problems.description:
Read an integer item count and a float unit price from one line separated by a space. Multiply them, then print the total and its runtime type using type() - exactly as a till multiplies quantity by price and the result lands in a decimal money type.

Sample Input: 4 12.5
Expected Output: Total: 50.0 | Type: <class 'float'>
criteria: The count is converted with int() and the price with float() before multiplying
The type is printed with type(total), producing the literal <class 'float'>, not a hand-typed string
problems.hint: count, price = input().split(); then total = int(count) * float(price).

levels.title: User Input with input() & Type Casting
levels.topic:
Real-life analogy: Think of a microphone capturing raw audio as text. Before a synthesizer can play it back as musical notes, that text has to be converted into numerical pitch frequencies - the raw capture alone is not a number.

input() always returns a str, no matter what the user types. Before any arithmetic you must cast it with int() or float(); skipping the cast either raises a TypeError or silently does string work ("20" * 3) instead of maths.

problems.title: Age Verification Scanner
problems.description:
Read a name and a birth year separated by a space. Convert the birth year to an int, compute the age assuming the current year is 2026, and print the summary line - the same check a sign-up form runs before it lets someone register.

Sample Input: Ali 2004
Expected Output: User Ali is 22 years old.
criteria: The birth year is converted with int() before the subtraction (2026 - year), never left as a string
For input "Ali 2004" the program prints exactly "User Ali is 22 years old."
problems.hint: name, year = input().split(); age = 2026 - int(year).

levels.title: String Slicing & f-Strings
levels.topic:
Real-life analogy: Think of cutting one specific rectangular frame out of a long film strip (slicing), then laying a dynamic subtitle over that frame (an f-string).

Strings are immutable sequences. The slice str[start:stop:step] returns a new substring without changing the original, and an f-string f"{value}" drops variables straight into text - faster and clearer than + concatenation.

problems.title: Product SKU Code Parser
problems.description:
Read a SKU string in the form SKU-9481-PKG. Slice out just the 4-digit product ID in the middle and print it behind a # using an f-string - the way a warehouse scanner pulls the item number out of a longer barcode label.

Sample Input: SKU-9481-PKG
Expected Output: Parsed Product ID: #9481
criteria: The 4 digits are extracted with slice notation (e.g. sku[4:8]), not a hard-coded "9481"
The result is printed via an f-string, producing exactly "Parsed Product ID: #9481"
problems.hint: sku[4:8] grabs the four characters after "SKU-"; then print(f"Parsed Product ID: #{pid}").

levels.title: Decision Structures (if, elif, else)
levels.topic:
Real-life analogy: Think of an automated postal sorting machine dropping each letter into the local, domestic or international chute based on its postcode - one letter, exactly one chute.

if tests a condition; elif checks the next one only when every earlier test failed; else catches everything left over. Conditions use comparison operators (< > == !=) and can be combined with the logical operators and, or and not.

problems.title: Speed Radar Enforcer
problems.description:
Read a single integer speed. Print NORMAL if it is 80 or below, WARNING if it is 81 to 100, and PENALTY if it is above 100 - the exact three-band decision a roadside speed camera makes on every car.

Sample Input: 95
Expected Output: WARNING
criteria: The three outcomes form one if / elif / else chain, not three separate independent if statements
For input 95 the program prints exactly "WARNING", and only one band ever prints per input
problems.hint: if speed <= 80: ... elif speed <= 100: ... else: ...

levels.title: Iteration with for & while Loops
levels.topic:
Real-life analogy: Think of a quality-control conveyor belt that examines every box in turn, and keeps going until someone hits the emergency stop button.

A for loop steps over a range or a collection a known number of times; a while loop repeats as long as its condition stays true. break leaves the loop early and continue skips straight to the next iteration.

problems.title: Even Sequence Accumulator
problems.description:
Read a single integer N. Loop through 1 to N with range(), add up only the even numbers, and print the total - a meter that ticks forward only on every second unit.

Sample Input: 10
Expected Output: Even Sum: 30
criteria: A loop over range() walks 1..N and an even test (n % 2 == 0) decides what gets added
For N = 10 the program prints exactly "Even Sum: 30" (2 + 4 + 6 + 8 + 10)
problems.hint: total = 0; for n in range(1, N + 1): if n % 2 == 0: total += n.

levels.title: Lists & List Comprehensions
levels.topic:
Real-life analogy: Think of a digital shopping cart you can add to, remove from, reorder, or run a bulk discount across in a single pass.

A list is a mutable, ordered sequence. A comprehension [expr for x in iterable if cond] builds a whole new list in one readable line, replacing the append-inside-a-loop pattern.

problems.title: Squares of Odds Generator
problems.description:
Read a line of space-separated integers. Using a single list comprehension, square only the odd values and print the resulting list - one pass over the belt that keeps the odd items and transforms them.

Sample Input: 1 2 3 4
Expected Output: [1, 9]
criteria: One list comprehension does both the odd filter (if n % 2) and the squaring (n ** 2) - no manual loop with .append()
For input "1 2 3 4" the program prints exactly "[1, 9]"
problems.hint: [n ** 2 for n in nums if n % 2].

levels.title: Tuples & Sets
levels.topic:
Real-life analogy: Think of a sealed birth certificate that can never be edited (a tuple), and an automated party guestbook that silently refuses to write down a name it already has (a set).

A tuple (x, y) is an immutable record - fixed the moment it is created. A set {a, b} stores only unique values and offers O(1) membership tests plus set algebra (union, intersection, difference).

problems.title: Duplicate Identifier Filter
problems.description:
Read a line of space-separated integers that may contain repeats. Convert to a set to drop the duplicates, then print the unique count and the sorted list of unique values - a turnstile that counts each distinct badge only once.

Sample Input: 5 2 5 8 2
Expected Output: Unique Count: 3 | Unique Elements: [2, 5, 8]
criteria: Duplicates are removed by converting to a set, not by a manual membership loop
The unique values are passed through sorted() for display, printing exactly "Unique Count: 3 | Unique Elements: [2, 5, 8]"
problems.hint: uniq = set(nums); then len(uniq) and sorted(uniq).

levels.title: Dictionaries & Key-Value Lookups
levels.topic:
Real-life analogy: Think of a physical telephone directory - you look up a contact name and get their number instantly, without scanning every page one by one.

A dictionary {key: value} stores pairs and finds a value by key in near-constant time. .get() reads safely with a fallback, and .keys(), .values() and .items() let you iterate the parts.

problems.title: Word Frequency Counter
criteria: Counts are built in a dict, incrementing per word (d[w] = d.get(w, 0) + 1 or similar) - not a fixed set of named variables
For input "apple banana apple" the program prints exactly "{'apple': 2, 'banana': 1}"
problems.hint: for w in text.split(): freq[w] = freq.get(w, 0) + 1.

levels.title: Defining Functions & Default Arguments
levels.topic:
Real-life analogy: Think of a coffee vending machine with recipe buttons. Press Espresso and it uses the standard recipe; or optionally dial in a custom sugar level before you press.

def names a reusable block that takes parameters and hands back a result with return. A default argument (people=2) makes a parameter optional, and defaults must come after all the required parameters in the signature.

problems.title: Bill Splitter Function
problems.description:
Write a function split_bill(amount, people=2) that returns each person's share. Read an amount and a people count, call the function, and print the per-person share formatted to 2 decimal places - the same split a group does over a restaurant bill.

Sample Input: 150 3
Expected Output: Share per person: $50.00
criteria: split_bill is a def with people defaulting to 2 (def split_bill(amount, people=2)), and the share is returned, not printed inside the function
The share is formatted to exactly 2 decimals, printing "Share per person: $50.00" for input "150 3"
problems.hint: def split_bill(amount, people=2): return amount / people  - then print(f"Share per person: ${share:.2f}").

levels.title: *args, **kwargs & Variable Arguments
levels.topic:
Real-life analogy: Think of an open grocery bag that stretches to hold any number of items (*args), plus a box of labelled gift tags where each tag has a name and a value (**kwargs).

*args collects any extra positional arguments into a tuple; **kwargs collects any extra named arguments into a dict. Together they let one function accept a variable number of inputs.

problems.title: Dynamic Math Product Engine
problems.description:
Write a function product_all(*numbers) that multiplies every argument it receives and returns the total. Read a line of space-separated integers, unpack them into the call, and print the combined product - a till that multiplies however many quantities you hand it.

Sample Input: 2 3 4 5
Expected Output: Combined Product: 120
criteria: product_all is defined with *numbers and works for any count of arguments, not a fixed a, b, c, d list
For input "2 3 4 5" the program prints exactly "Combined Product: 120"
problems.hint: def product_all(*numbers): total = 1; for n in numbers: total *= n; return total  - call product_all(*nums).

levels.title: Lambda Expressions & Scope (LEGB)
levels.topic:
Real-life analogy: Think of a disposable sticky-note calculation you use once and throw away - and you always check your own desk notes before walking over to the office noticeboard.

A lambda is a small anonymous function written inline: lambda x: x * 2. Name lookup follows LEGB - Local, then Enclosing, then Global, then Built-in - so an inner scope can see outer names but not the other way round.

problems.title: Custom Key Sorter
problems.description:
Read pairs of name and age from one line (name age name age ...). Build a list of (name, age) tuples and sort it by age ascending using a lambda key in sorted(), then print the sorted list - a leaderboard reordering itself by score.

Sample Input: Bob 30 Alice 25 Charlie 35
Expected Output: [('Alice', 25), ('Bob', 30), ('Charlie', 35)]
criteria: sorted() is called with key=lambda t: t[1], so the sort is by age, not by name or the whole tuple
For the sample input the program prints exactly "[('Alice', 25), ('Bob', 30), ('Charlie', 35)]"
problems.hint: sorted(pairs, key=lambda t: t[1]).

levels.title: Classes, Objects & __init__
levels.topic:
Real-life analogy: Think of an architect's blueprint that defines what every car has, versus each physical car rolling off the production line built from that one blueprint.

A class bundles data (attributes) and behaviour (methods). __init__(self, ...) runs automatically when an object is created and sets up its starting state; self is the current object, passed first to every method.

problems.title: Student Profile Manager
problems.description:
Create a Student class with a name and a gpa attribute set in __init__, and a display() method that prints the profile line. Read a name and a GPA, build one Student, and call display() - a records system printing one student card.

Sample Input: Sara 3.85
Expected Output: Student: Sara | GPA: 3.85
criteria: name and gpa are assigned in __init__ as self.name / self.gpa, and display() is a method that reads them via self
For input "Sara 3.85" calling display() prints exactly "Student: Sara | GPA: 3.85"
problems.hint: In __init__: self.name = name and self.gpa = gpa; then def display(self): print(f"Student: {self.name} | GPA: {self.gpa}").

levels.title: Inheritance & Polymorphism
levels.topic:
Real-life analogy: Think of a smart tablet that inherits every standard smartphone feature, then adds stylus support and a larger screen on top.

class Child(Parent) reuses the parent's code. super().__init__() runs the parent constructor so the child does not repeat that setup, and a child can override a method to change its behaviour while callers keep using the same name.

problems.title: Employee Hierarchy Manager
problems.description:
Create a base Employee class holding name and salary, and a derived Manager class that adds a department and calls super().__init__(). Read a name, salary and department, build one Manager, and print its summary line - an org-chart entry for a manager.

Sample Input: Daniel 85000 Engineering
Expected Output: Manager: Daniel | Salary: $85000 | Dept: Engineering
criteria: Manager(Employee) subclasses Employee and calls super().__init__(name, salary) rather than re-assigning name/salary itself
For the sample input the program prints exactly "Manager: Daniel | Salary: $85000 | Dept: Engineering"
problems.hint: class Manager(Employee): def __init__(self, name, salary, dept): super().__init__(name, salary); then self.dept = dept.

levels.title: File Handling with 'with' & Exceptions
levels.topic:
Real-life analogy: Think of an automated vault door that unlocks as you step in and swings shut and locks itself the moment you leave - you never have to remember to close it.

with open(path) as f: guarantees the file is closed even if an error strikes mid-block. try / except / finally catches failures (a missing file, a bad value) so the program recovers instead of crashing.

problems.title: Safe Log File Writer & Reader
problems.description:
Read one line of text. Inside a with block, write it to server.log; then reopen the file in read mode inside another with block and print its contents behind a label - the capstone finale, combining file writing, guaranteed closing and safe reading into one round trip, exactly like a vault that locks itself between visits.

Sample Input: STATUS_PORT_8080_ACTIVE
Expected Output: Log File Content: STATUS_PORT_8080_ACTIVE
criteria: Both the write and the read happen inside with open(...) blocks (no manual f.close()), writing in "w" mode and reading in the default read mode
For input "STATUS_PORT_8080_ACTIVE" the program prints exactly "Log File Content: STATUS_PORT_8080_ACTIVE"
problems.hint: with open("server.log", "w") as f: f.write(text)  then  with open("server.log") as f: print("Log File Content:", f.read()).

catalogue.title: CS-105: Fundamentals of JavaScript
catalogue.summary: The JavaScript engine and console.log() through scoping, type coercion, arrays and objects to closures, currying and asynchronous code with Promises and async/await, with a real-life analogy, a video, and a scenario-based Compiler Quest for every one of 15 topics across 5 modules.

track.title: CS-105: Fundamentals of JavaScript
track.description: The language of the browser and the server. From the JavaScript engine and console.log() through scoping, type coercion, arrays and objects to closures, currying and asynchronous code with Promises, async/await and the Fetch API. Five modules, fifteen topics, one real-life analogy, one video and one scenario-based Compiler Quest each, every quest with an exact Sample Input and Expected Output - certificate at the end.
track.outcome: Run JavaScript in an engine and log structured diagnostics; use let/const scoping, the seven primitive types and explicit conversion, and strict versus loose equality deliberately; build strings with template literals and iterate data with for...of / for...in / while; transform data with map, filter and reduce, and reshape it with destructuring, spread and JSON deep cloning; write arrow functions with lexical this, closures with private state and curried higher-order functions; reason about the event loop, and handle asynchronous work with Promises, async/await, try...catch and Promise.all().

levels.title: JS Runtime Engine & console.log()
levels.topic:
Real-life analogy: Think of a live theatre prompter whispering each line to the actors in real time, handling backstage cues on the spot and jotting the stage status straight into the stage manager's notebook.

JavaScript runs inside an engine - V8 in Chrome and Node.js, SpiderMonkey in Firefox - executing statements one after another on a single-threaded call stack. console.log() streams formatted diagnostic output to the developer console, and passing it several comma-separated arguments prints them on one line separated by spaces.

problems.title: System Startup Diagnostic Banner
problems.description:
Use console.log() to print an engine initialization line, then a second line built from comma-separated arguments for the status and mode - the prompter logging the stage status before the show begins.

Input: None
Expected Output:
[V8 Engine] Core Initialized
Status: Online, Mode: Production
criteria: The second line is produced by passing console.log() comma-separated arguments (e.g. "Status: Online," then "Mode: Production"), not one pre-joined string
The output is exactly two lines: "[V8 Engine] Core Initialized" then "Status: Online, Mode: Production"
problems.hint: console.log("[V8 Engine] Core Initialized"); then console.log("Status: Online,", "Mode: Production");

levels.title: Variable Scoping (let, const, var) & Hoisting
levels.topic:
Real-life analogy: Think of var as a megaphone heard across the whole floor (function-scoped), let as a conversation inside a soundproof meeting room (block-scoped), and const as a permanent engraved metal plaque.

Modern JavaScript uses let (reassignable, block-scoped) and const (block-scoped, its binding fixed once assigned). var is hoisted to the top of its function and ignores { } block boundaries, which quietly leaks values across scopes and causes bugs.

problems.title: Block-Scoped Tax Calculator
problems.description:
Declare a const TAX_RATE = 0.08. Read a price, and inside a { } block use let to compute the taxed total, formatting it to 2 decimal places behind a dollar sign - the calculation staying inside its own soundproof room.

Sample Input: 100
Expected Output: Total with Tax: $108.00
criteria: TAX_RATE is a const and the total is computed with let inside a block, using price * (1 + TAX_RATE)
For input 100 the program prints exactly "Total with Tax: $108.00" (with the two decimal places)
problems.hint: const total = price * (1 + TAX_RATE); then total.toFixed(2) for the 2-decimal string.

levels.title: Primitive Data Types & Type Conversion
levels.topic:
Real-life analogy: Think of an international exchange booth: the machines turn number vouchers into text tickets and back, but hand you an empty "Rejected" slip (NaN) when the input makes no sense.

JavaScript has seven primitive types: string, number, bigint, boolean, undefined, symbol and null. typeof reports a value's type, and Number(), String() and Boolean() convert explicitly between them.

problems.title: Type Inspector & Parser
problems.description:
Read a numeric string such as "45". Convert it to a real number with Number(), multiply by 2, then print the result and its typeof - the exchange booth turning a text ticket into a spendable number.

Sample Input: "45"
Expected Output: Result: 90 | Type: number
criteria: The string is converted with Number() (or parseInt / parseFloat) before the multiplication - it is not multiplied as a string
For input "45" the program prints exactly "Result: 90 | Type: number", where the type comes from typeof
problems.hint: const n = Number(raw); then typeof (n * 2) is "number".

levels.title: Strict Equality (===) vs Loose Equality (==)
levels.topic:
Real-life analogy: Think of an airport checkpoint: loose equality (==) waves you through if the boarding pass merely looks close after some auto-adjusting; strict equality (===) demands the passport identity and an exact biometric match.

== coerces the two operands to a common type before comparing, so '5' == 5 is true and "0" == 0 is true. === compares type and value with no coercion, so '5' === 5 is false. Default to === everywhere.

problems.title: Coercion Sentinel Validator
problems.description:
Compare the string "0" against the number 0 with both == and ===, and print the two boolean results on one line - showing where loose equality lets a mismatch slip past the gate that strict equality stops.

Input: None
Expected Output: Loose: true | Strict: false
criteria: Both "0" == 0 and "0" === 0 are actually evaluated (not hard-coded booleans), and their results are printed
The program prints exactly "Loose: true | Strict: false"
problems.hint: console.log(`Loose: ${"0" == 0} | Strict: ${"0" === 0}`);

levels.title: Template Literals & String Methods
levels.topic:
Real-life analogy: Think of a fill-in-the-blank invitation card where the name, the date and the RSVP link snap automatically into their pre-cut slots.

Template literals use backticks and support multi-line text and ${expr} interpolation directly inside the string. Common string methods include includes(), slice(), trim() and replace() / replaceAll().

problems.title: Dynamic URL Query Builder
problems.description:
Read a host, an endpoint and an id. Using a single template literal, assemble a clean HTTPS API URL with the id as a query parameter - the invitation card dropping each value into its slot.

Sample Input: "api.site.com" "users" 101
Expected Output: Endpoint: https://api.site.com/users?id=101
criteria: The URL is built with one backtick template literal using ${...} interpolation, not string + concatenation
For the sample input the program prints exactly "Endpoint: https://api.site.com/users?id=101"
problems.hint: `Endpoint: https://${host}/${endpoint}?id=${id}`

levels.title: Iteration (for...of, for...in, while)
levels.topic:
Real-life analogy: Think of a bookshelf: for...of walks past every physical book in turn, while for...in reads the little index tags stuck to the shelf frame itself.

for...of iterates the values of an iterable (arrays, strings, sets). for...in iterates the enumerable keys of an object. while repeats its body as long as its condition stays truthy.

problems.title: Array Value Accumulator
problems.description:
Given an array of integers, use a for...of loop to add every element into a running total, then print the sum - stepping past each book on the shelf and tallying as you go.

Sample Input: [10, 20, 30, 40]
Expected Output: Sum: 100
criteria: The total is accumulated with a for...of loop over the values - not for...in, and not .reduce() here
For [10, 20, 30, 40] the program prints exactly "Sum: 100"
problems.hint: let sum = 0; for (const n of arr) sum += n;

levels.title: Modern Array Methods (map, filter, reduce)
levels.topic:
Real-life analogy: Think of a car assembly line: map sprays every car the same colour, filter pulls the defective ones off the belt, and reduce adds every remaining car's value into one fleet total.

Higher-order array methods build immutable pipelines: map() returns a new array with each element transformed, filter() returns a new array of the elements that pass a test, and reduce() folds the array into a single accumulated value.

problems.title: Even Square Reducer
problems.description:
Starting from [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6], use filter() to keep the even numbers, map() to square them, and reduce() to sum the squares into one total - the assembly line transforming, rejecting and totalling in one chain.

Input: None
Expected Output: Reduced Total: 56
criteria: The result comes from a chained filter() -> map() -> reduce() with no manual for loop and accumulator
The program prints exactly "Reduced Total: 56" (2*2 + 4*4 + 6*6)

levels.title: Objects, Destructuring & Spread / Rest (...)
levels.topic:
Real-life analogy: Think of unpacking a flat-pack furniture crate: you lift the desk top and legs straight out by name (destructuring), and sweep the leftover screws into a spare-parts bag (rest).

Destructuring pulls properties or elements into their own variables (const { name, age } = user;). The spread operator ... copies or merges objects and arrays; rest ... in a parameter or pattern collects whatever is left over.

problems.title: Object Merge & Destructure
criteria: The two objects are combined with { ...a, ...b } and the three fields are pulled out by destructuring, not dot access one by one
For the sample input the program prints exactly "User #1: a@b.com (Dev)"
problems.hint: const { id, email, role } = { ...objA, ...objB }; then `User #${id}: ${email} (${role})`.

levels.title: JSON Serialization & Deep Cloning
levels.topic:
Real-life analogy: Think of flat-packing a wardrobe into a cardboard box to mail across the country (serialization), then building an identical wardrobe at the other end (deserialization).

JSON.stringify() turns an object into a JSON string; JSON.parse() turns it back into an object. Parsing a stringified copy - or structuredClone() - gives a genuine deep copy that shares no references with the original.

problems.title: JSON Data Roundtrip
problems.description:
Create an object holding a value of 100. Deep-clone it by JSON.stringify then JSON.parse, change the clone's value to 200, and print both to prove the original was untouched - the mailed wardrobe rebuilt as a separate piece of furniture.

Input: None
Expected Output: Original: 100 | Cloned: 200
criteria: The clone is made via JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(obj)) or structuredClone - not by assigning the object to another variable
After mutating only the clone, the program prints exactly "Original: 100 | Cloned: 200"
problems.hint: const clone = JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(obj)); clone.value = 200;

levels.title: Arrow Functions & the 'this' Keyword
levels.topic:
Real-life analogy: Think of a regular function as an actor whose identity shifts with whatever stage they stand on, and an arrow function as a reporter who always speaks with the voice of the home office they came from.

Arrow functions - const fn = (a, b) => a + b - are concise and, crucially, take this from the scope where they are defined rather than how they are called. A single-expression body has an implicit return with no braces.

problems.title: Concise Arrow Multiplier
problems.description:
Write an arrow function with an implicit return that computes the area of a rectangle from its two sides. Read two numbers, call it, and print the area.

Sample Input: 6 7
Expected Output: Area: 42
criteria: The function is an arrow function with an implicit return (no return keyword, no { } body): const area = (w, h) => w * h
For input "6 7" the program prints exactly "Area: 42"
problems.hint: const area = (w, h) => w * h; - no braces means the value is returned automatically.

levels.title: Closures & Encapsulation (Private State)
levels.topic:
Real-life analogy: Think of a bank teller who keeps the vault combination in their head: customers deposit and withdraw through the window and never touch the dials themselves.

A closure lets an inner function keep using variables from its outer function's scope even after that outer function has returned. Returning the inner function (or an object of them) creates truly private state that outside code cannot reach directly.

problems.title: Private Counter Closure
problems.description:
Write a factory createCounter() that keeps a private count starting at 0 and returns a function which increments and returns it each time it is called. Call the returned function three times and print the values on one line - the teller's dials stay behind the window.

Input: None (call 3 times)
Expected Output: 1 2 3
criteria: count is a variable inside createCounter (not a property on the returned function or a global), reachable only through the returned closure
Calling the returned function three times yields exactly "1 2 3"
problems.hint: function createCounter() { let count = 0; return () => ++count; }

levels.title: Higher-Order Functions & Currying
levels.topic:
Real-life analogy: Think of a build-your-own sandwich line: one station takes your bread choice, the next your protein, the next your sauce - each takes a single decision and passes the sandwich along.

A higher-order function takes a function as an argument or returns one. Currying rewrites a multi-argument function f(a, b, c) as a chain of one-argument functions f(a)(b)(c), which makes partial application and composition natural.

problems.title: Curried Discount Calculator
problems.description:
Write a curried function applyDiscount = discount => price => price - price * discount. Read a discount rate and a price, apply the discount in two calls, and print the final price - each station on the line taking one value.

Sample Input: 0.10 200
Expected Output: Final Price: $180
criteria: applyDiscount is curried: it takes the discount first and returns a function that takes the price, called as applyDiscount(rate)(price)
For input "0.10 200" the program prints exactly "Final Price: $180"
problems.hint: const applyDiscount = discount => price => price - price * discount; then applyDiscount(0.10)(200).

levels.title: Event Loop, Callbacks & the Call Stack
levels.topic:
Real-life analogy: Think of one busy chef (the call stack). When a dish needs 20 minutes in the oven (a Web API), the chef starts it and cooks other orders, only plating the baked dish once the timer rings and the queue hands it back.

JavaScript runs on one thread. Asynchronous work is handed to the browser or Node APIs, and its callbacks wait in a task queue; the event loop only pushes a queued callback onto the call stack once the stack is empty - so setTimeout(fn, 0) still runs after all the synchronous code.

problems.title: Non-Blocking setTimeout Ordering
problems.description:
Print "A", schedule a setTimeout(..., 0) that prints "B", then print "C". Show the real execution order - the chef finishing the quick dishes before the oven timer rings.

Input: None
Expected Output:
A
C
B
criteria: "B" is printed from inside a setTimeout(..., 0) callback, while "A" and "C" are printed synchronously
The program prints the three letters in the order A, then C, then B (one per line)
problems.hint: console.log("A"); setTimeout(() => console.log("B"), 0); console.log("C"); - the timer callback always waits for the stack to clear.

levels.title: Promises (.then, .catch, .finally)
levels.topic:
Real-life analogy: Think of the buzzer they hand you at a burger counter. It is a promise: right now Pending, it will Resolve into a hot meal when ready, or Reject if the kitchen runs out of patties.

A Promise represents a value that will arrive later. It is Pending, then either Fulfilled or Rejected. .then() handles the resolved value, .catch() handles a rejection, and .finally() runs cleanup either way.

problems.title: Promise Resolution Engine
problems.description:
Create a Promise that resolves with "Data Loaded". Attach .then() to print it behind a [Resolved] label and .finally() to print a cleanup line - the buzzer going off with a finished meal, then the tray being cleared.

Sample Input: Success
Expected Output:
[Resolved] Data Loaded
[Cleanup] Stream Closed
criteria: The resolved value is read in .then() and the cleanup line runs in .finally() - not just two console.logs in sequence
The program prints exactly two lines: "[Resolved] Data Loaded" then "[Cleanup] Stream Closed"
problems.hint: Promise.resolve("Data Loaded").then(v => console.log(`[Resolved] ${v}`)).finally(() => console.log("[Cleanup] Stream Closed"));

levels.title: Modern async / await & the Fetch API
levels.topic:
Real-life analogy: Think of reading a book of clear step-by-step instructions top to bottom. An assistant is fetching reference notes in the background, but your reading stays linear - no tangle of nested callbacks.

async/await is synchronous-looking syntax over Promises: await pauses an async function until a Promise settles, and try...catch handles failures. Promise.all() runs several async operations at once and waits for all of them.

problems.title: Async/Await HTTP Request Handler
criteria: The function is declared async and uses await on the simulated fetch inside a try...catch block, not .then() chains
For a 200 response the program prints exactly 'Response: 200 | Payload: {"status": "success"}'
problems.hint: async function handle() { try { const res = await fakeFetch(); console.log(`Response: ${res.code} | Payload: ${JSON.stringify(res.body)}`); } catch (e) { /* fallback */ } }

catalogue.title: CS-106: Fundamentals of HTML & CSS

track.title: CS-106: Fundamentals of HTML & CSS
track.description: Core front-end foundations - build accessible, standards-compliant web pages from scratch: HTML document structure, semantic markup, tables and forms, then CSS selectors, the box model, display and positioning, Flexbox and Grid, and mobile-first responsive design with motion. Five modules, fifteen topics, one real-life analogy, one video and one scenario-based Compiler Quest each, every quest with an exact Sample Input and Expected Output - certificate at the end.
track.outcome: Write a valid HTML5 document with correct nesting, headings, lists, links and accessible images; structure a page with semantic landmarks, data tables and validation-ready forms; apply CSS by selector, style colour, units and typography, and reason about the box model; control layout with display and positioning, centre and space with Flexbox, and compose two-dimensional layouts with Grid; make a page mobile-first responsive with media queries, add tasteful reduced-motion-aware animation, and ship a complete responsive landing page.

levels.title: HTML Boilerplate & Document Anatomy
levels.topic:
Real-life analogy: Think of the blueprint and foundation of a house. Before any furniture or paint, you pour the concrete slab (doctype), raise the frame (html), route the hidden utilities in the basement (head), and define the living space people actually walk through (body).

Every HTML page begins with <!DOCTYPE html> and a root html element containing a head for metadata (title, charset, viewport) and a body for visible content. Proper nesting and the lang attribute give browsers and screen readers a reliable structure to parse.

problems.title: Minimal Valid Page
problems.description:
Build a valid HTML5 page whose browser tab reads EchoLens and whose body shows a single h1 greeting - the foundation poured before anything else goes on top.

Sample Input: BuildPage
Expected Output: Tab title: EchoLens | Page heading: Hello EchoLens
criteria: The document has <!DOCTYPE html>, then <html> > <head> (with a <title>) > <body>, correctly nested
The <title> is exactly "EchoLens" and the body contains one <h1> reading "Hello EchoLens"
problems.hint: <title> goes inside <head>; the visible greeting goes in an <h1> inside <body>.

levels.title: Text Content Elements (headings, paragraphs, lists)
levels.topic:
Real-life analogy: Think of laying out a newspaper page. The masthead is the biggest headline (h1), section titles are sub-headlines (h2, h3), body columns are paragraphs, and bullet briefs are lists down the margin. Headings h1 to h6 express document hierarchy,

holds paragraphs, and

problems.title: Recipe Card
problems.description:
Mark up a recipe with a title, a short intro paragraph, and an ordered list of exactly three steps - the headline, the standfirst and the numbered how-to.

Sample Input: BuildRecipe
Expected Output: One heading, one paragraph, and a numbered 1-2-3 step list
criteria:
There is exactly one heading (e.g.

), one

intro, and an

    (not a
      ) for the steps
The <ol> contains exactly three <li> items, so the browser numbers them 1, 2, 3
problems.hint: Use <ol> for steps that have an order; each step is its own <li>.

levels.title: Links, Images & Attributes
levels.topic: Real-life analogy: Think of a hotel concierge. Links are directions to other destinations (href), images are framed photographs on the wall, and the alt text is the caption a guide reads aloud to a visitor who cannot see the picture. The element navigates to internal or external destinations, while embeds images with a mandatory alt attribute for accessibility. Attributes such as target and rel control how resources open and behave.

problems.title: Linked Logo
problems.description:
Wrap an image in a link that opens the EchoLens site in a new tab, with proper alt text on the image - the framed photo that is also a doorway to somewhere else.

Sample Input: LinkLogo
Expected Output: Clickable logo image opens a new tab, alt text present
criteria: An with a non-empty, meaningful alt attribute is nested inside an pointing at the EchoLens site
The link opens in a new tab via target="_blank" and carries rel="noopener"

levels.title: Semantic Layout Elements
levels.topic:
Real-life analogy: Think of posting clear signs on the rooms of a house. Instead of calling every space a generic room, you label them: Entrance (header), Hallway (nav), Living Room (main), Store Room (aside), Exit (footer).

Semantic tags header, nav, main, section, article, aside and footer describe the meaning of page regions. They improve accessibility, SEO and maintainability compared with generic <div> containers.

problems.title: Semantic Skeleton
problems.description:
Rebuild a <div>-only layout using header, nav, main and footer landmarks with identical visuals - the same rooms, now with signs on the doors.

Sample Input: Semanticize
Expected Output: Same visual layout, now built from meaningful semantic region tags
criteria: <header>, <nav>, <main> and <footer> replace the generic <div>s, each used for the region that matches its meaning
The rendered layout looks identical to the div version - only the tag names changed
problems.hint: header wraps the top, nav wraps the link list, main wraps the primary content, footer wraps the bottom.

levels.title: Tables & Structured Data
levels.topic:
Real-life analogy: Think of a train timetable board at a station. Column headers name each track and time, rows list each departure, and the grid lets a traveller cross-reference destination against schedule instantly.

Tables use table, thead, tbody, tr, th and td to present two-dimensional data. A <caption> names the table and th scope="col" ties each data cell to its column header for assistive technology.

problems.title: Price Table
problems.description:
Build a 3-row pricing table with a header row and a descriptive caption - the timetable board with its title and column labels.

Sample Input: BuildTable
Expected Output: A bordered table with a header row, 3 data rows, and a caption
criteria: The <table> has a <caption>, a header row of <th> cells inside <thead>, and exactly 3 data rows of <td> inside <tbody>
Each header <th> uses scope="col"
